prompt: Run the llm-straighten and llm-network-loop LLM ablation baselines for as-twn-taipei, variant orig-llm-working2grid-opus5, as a forced re-run from scratch: reset each chain first, then decide every grid coordinate by hand-reasoning (no algorithm), and make sure a complete, rule-compliant assignment is actually applied rather than handing back an analysis.

transcript.note: Round 0, note only (no moves, so this does not count as a round). The straightening handed me a 55x60 grid with 32 empty columns and 38 empty rows -- more than half of each axis is dead space, which is an artefact of the rank-based gridding, not something I should be hand-fixing vertex by vertex. compactGridSafe removes exactly those bands and is rank-preserving, so it cannot break an alignment or reorder anything. I am therefore letting the program squeeze the grid first and reading the result back, because every distance in the layout changes: a segment whose endpoints were 11 columns apart in the sparse grid may be 3 apart afterwards, which is what decides whether an H/V snap is reachable inside the short-distance limit at all. Proposing moves against the sparse coordinates first would have me judging reachability against distances that are about to disappear.

Round 1 on the compacted 23x22 grid. First, a measurement that set my whole strategy: compaction dropped HVD from 71 to 68 while leaving HV at 65 untouched. That is structural -- removing bands is rank-preserving, so 'same row' and 'same column' survive, but 'equal dc and dr' does not. So every 45deg I buy in this chain is liable to be destroyed by the compaction at the end of the same apply, while every H/V is permanent. I therefore spent this round on HV and on grid size, and deliberately did NOT chase diagonal upgrades. (a) HV: 42 (Luzhou, a degree-1 terminus) hangs off 39 at (-3,2). 39 cannot move -- both of its segments are horizontal on row 13, and its column is boxed between 16 at col 13 and 25 at col 16 -- and a horizontal 39-42 is impossible because the segment would swallow 16. So the only H/V is a vertical, which needs 42 on col 14: I put it at (14,14) rather than (14,15) because that also empties row 15. (b) Grid shrink -- I went looking for rows and columns held open by a single vertex that could step aside without breaking anything, and found six. 55 is degree 2 with both segments vertical on col 22, so its row is free: (22,11) vacates row 12 and keeps 34 < 55 < 32 in order. 8, 37, 19 and 56 are all degree-1 stubs whose single segment is vertical, so sliding each one cell along its own column keeps it H/V while vacating rows 3, 6, 17 and 19 -- each time I moved it AWAY from its parent, never onto it, and checked the lengthened segment does not swallow the cell it left. (c) Column 17 was held open by five vertices, so I emptied it as a block: 12/40/10/9 are a rigid vertical chain (40-12, 40-10, 10-9 all V) and move together to col 18, where rows 9/10/11/13 are free; every horizontal they carry (23-12, 22-12, 44-40, 40-17, 24-10, 30-10, 25-9) keeps its row, so nothing is lost, and after compaction those segments are no longer than before. The fifth occupant, stub 5, steps the other way to (16,4), keeping 6-5 horizontal. Net: HV 65 -> 66, and 23x22 should compact to 21x16 (columns 11 and 17 and rows 3, 6, 12, 15, 17, 19 all fall out). Pre-checked: cross 0, vtxOn 0, collide 0, no winding-order violations, orderFlip 7.

Round 2 on the 21x16 grid. Round 1 taught me the pattern that pays here: a column or row is usually held open by ONE vertex whose own segments are all perpendicular to the direction it needs to move, so it can slide along and stay H/V. I swept every axis for that case. Seven columns fell to it: 11, 43 and 4 all sit on a locked row with two horizontal neighbours, so their columns are free and each can step to col 4 as long as it stays between its two neighbours (11 must stay between 7 at col 0 and 15 at col 8; 43 and 4 likewise) -- that empties cols 2, 3 and 5 into one shared column. 29 steps west to col 6 (emptying col 7), 1 steps east to col 11 (emptying col 10) and stub 41 steps east to col 19 (emptying col 18); in each case I moved it AWAY from its partner so the lengthened segment cannot swallow the cell it vacated, and checked the vacated cell is not left sitting on some other line. Two rows fell to the same trick: row 1 was held by the two stubs 14 and 21, and both hang below a vertical partner, so dropping each to row 0 keeps them vertical and clears row 1; row 3 was held by stub 8 plus the rigid pair 6-5, and 6 can only go to row 2 (row 4 is taken by 13 on its own column), so I moved 5 and 6 down together and 8 up to row 4. (b) The one alignment gain: 2-18 was a 45deg before the last compaction and got flattened to (-2,1) by it. 2's column is pinned by the 2-3 vertical, so I moved 2 and 3 together one column west to 13, which restores 2-18 to (-1,1) AND empties col 14 -- the same move buys both objectives. (c) Trade-off I accepted knowingly: emptying col 10 shortens 16-33 from (-4,-4) to (-3,-4), i.e. it costs the 16-33 diagonal. I took the column anyway, because the loop's own stop condition counts grid dimensions as an objective while 45deg is the weakest term in the score, and my compaction preview showed the total holds at HVD 69 regardless -- the same band removal happens to pull 45-36 onto (3,3), so one diagonal replaces the other. Predicted result 21x16 -> 14x14 with HV unchanged at 66. Pre-checked on both the pre- and post-compaction layouts: cross 0, vtxOn 0, collide 0, no winding-order violations, and no segment reverses the sign of its dx or dy (hard rule 2).
